bubble_sort.name: Bubble Sort
bubble_sort.purpose: Sort an array by repeatedly swapping adjacent elements that are out of order.
bubble_sort.problem_statement: Given an array of n comparable elements, arrange them in non-decreasing order.
bubble_sort.intuition: Like bubbles rising to the surface of water, the largest unsorted element floats to its correct position at the end of each pass.
bubble_sort.worked_example: Initial: [5, 1, 4, 2, 8]. Compare 5>1: swap -> [1, 5, 4, 2, 8]. Compare 5>4: swap -> [1, 4, 5, 2, 8]. Compare 5>2: swap -> [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]. Compare 5<8: ok -> [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]. Pass 1 places 8 at the end.
bubble_sort.time_complexity: Best: O(n) with early exit | Average: O(n²) | Worst: O(n²)
bubble_sort.stability: Stable (preserves relative order of equal items)
advantages: Simple to understand and implement.
Adaptive: O(n) when already sorted with early exit.
O(1) memory.
limitations: Inefficient O(n²) comparisons and swaps on large datasets.
Excessive swap operations.
bubble_sort.suitable_use_cases: Small lists or lists that are almost sorted.
common_mistakes: Off-by-one errors comparing j with j+1 beyond bounds.
bubble_sort.exam_observations: Number of comparisons in worst case: n(n-1)/2. Maximum swaps: n(n-1)/2.

selection_sort.name: Selection Sort
selection_sort.purpose: Sort an array by repeatedly finding the minimum element from the unsorted subarray and placing it at the beginning.
selection_sort.problem_statement: Partition array into sorted prefix and unsorted suffix; successively extract the minimum.
selection_sort.intuition: Select the smallest item and put it in place 0. Then select the second smallest and put it in place 1, and so on.
selection_sort.worked_example: Initial: [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]. Find min (10), swap with 29 -> [10, 29, 14, 37, 13]. Find min in remaining (13), swap with 29 -> [10, 13, 14, 37, 29].
selection_sort.time_complexity: Best: O(n²) | Average: O(n²) | Worst: O(n²)
selection_sort.stability: Unstable in standard array swap implementation.
advantages: Performs at most O(n) swaps, ideal when memory write operations are costly.
Simple and memory-efficient.
limitations: Always takes O(n²) comparisons even if input is already sorted.
Not stable.
selection_sort.suitable_use_cases: When memory write cycles are expensive (e.g. Flash EEPROM).
common_mistakes: Assuming it is O(n) on sorted input; it always scans all remaining elements.
selection_sort.exam_observations: Always performs exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons, but at most n-1 swaps.

insertion_sort.name: Insertion Sort
insertion_sort.purpose: Build the sorted array one element at a time by inserting each item into its correct relative position.
insertion_sort.problem_statement: Iteratively expand a sorted subarray by shifting larger elements right and inserting the current key.
insertion_sort.intuition: Similar to how people sort playing cards in their hands: take each card and slide it into its proper spot among previously sorted cards.
insertion_sort.time_complexity: Best: O(n) | Average: O(n²) | Worst: O(n²)
advantages: Linear O(n) time for nearly sorted inputs.
Online: can sort data as it arrives.
Low constant factor overhead.
limitations: O(n²) time on reverse or random large inputs.
insertion_sort.suitable_use_cases: Small arrays (often used as base case in hybrid sorts like Timsort) and nearly sorted data streams.
common_mistakes: Overwriting the key value before shifting elements.
insertion_sort.exam_observations: Number of inversions in the input equals the exact number of swap/shift operations.

merge_sort.name: Merge Sort
merge_sort.purpose: Sort an array using the divide-and-conquer paradigm by halving the array, sorting recursively, and merging sorted halves.
merge_sort.problem_statement: Recursively split array into halves until singletons remain, then merge them back in ordered sequence.
merge_sort.intuition: Merging two already sorted lists into one takes linear time O(n). Halving takes log n levels.
merge_sort.time_complexity: Best: O(n log n) | Average: O(n log n) | Worst: O(n log n)
merge_sort.space_complexity: O(n) Auxiliary space for merging buffers
advantages: Guaranteed O(n log n) worst-case time.
Stable sorting.
Well suited for external sorting on disk or linked lists.
limitations: Requires O(n) extra memory buffer.
Higher memory bandwidth usage than in-place sorts.
merge_sort.suitable_use_cases: Sorting linked lists, external sort of massive files, when guaranteed O(n log n) stability is required.
common_mistakes: Omitting base case (len <= 1), causing infinite recursion.
Memory leaks with auxiliary arrays in C++.
merge_sort.exam_observations: Recurrence relation: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). Solves to O(n log n) by Master Theorem (Case 2).

quick_sort.name: Quick Sort
quick_sort.purpose: Sort an array by partitioning elements around a chosen pivot, then recursively sorting sub-partitions.
quick_sort.problem_statement: Select pivot p; partition array so elements <= p are left and > p are right; recurse.
quick_sort.intuition: If we place one pivot in its absolute correct final position and partition around it, we divide the problem into two independent subproblems.
quick_sort.time_complexity: Best: O(n log n) | Average: O(n log n) | Worst: O(n²) with poor pivot
quick_sort.space_complexity: O(log n) call stack on average, O(n) worst case
advantages: Extremely fast in practice due to cache locality and low constants.
In-place partitioning.
limitations: Worst-case O(n²) when pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element.
Unstable.
quick_sort.suitable_use_cases: General-purpose in-memory sorting where average-case speed is critical.
common_mistakes: Not handling duplicate elements properly in partition loops.
Choosing fixed pivot on already sorted arrays.
quick_sort.exam_observations: Best/Average recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) -> O(n log n). Worst recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) -> O(n²).

heap_sort.name: Heap Sort
heap_sort.purpose: Sort an array using a binary heap data structure.
heap_sort.problem_statement: Build a Max-Heap in O(n) time, then repeatedly swap root with the end and max-heapify.
heap_sort.intuition: A Max-Heap always maintains the maximum element at the root (index 0). Swapping root to the end puts it in final position.
heap_sort.time_complexity: Best: O(n log n) | Average: O(n log n) | Worst: O(n log n)
advantages: Guaranteed O(n log n) without extra O(n) auxiliary memory.
Consistent performance without Quick Sort's worst case.
limitations: Poor CPU cache locality because heap navigation jumps across non-contiguous array indices.
Unstable.
heap_sort.suitable_use_cases: Embedded systems with tight memory limits requiring guaranteed O(n log n) worst-case time.
common_mistakes: Assuming building a heap takes O(n log n); building a heap takes O(n) time.
heap_sort.exam_observations: Building max-heap takes O(n) time. n-1 extractions each take O(log n), giving O(n log n) total.

bfs.name: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
bfs.purpose: Graph traversal exploring neighbor vertices level-by-level.
bfs.problem_statement: Given a start node, explore all reachable nodes in order of their distance (number of edges).
bfs.intuition: Waves expanding concentrically in water; checks all nodes at distance 1, then distance 2, etc.
bfs.worked_example: Queue start S. Pop S, push unvisited neighbors A, B. Pop A, push C. Pop B, push D. Visits level 1 before level 2.
bfs.space_complexity: O(V) for queue and visited set
bfs.stability: Guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs.
advantages: Finds shortest path in unweighted graphs.
Simple FIFO queue implementation.
limitations: High memory consumption: frontier grows exponentially with search depth.
Does not handle edge weights.
bfs.suitable_use_cases: Unweighted shortest paths, web crawling, social network degree of separation.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to mark nodes as visited when pushing to queue, causing duplicate processing.
bfs.exam_observations: Queue size can reach O(V) in worst case (e.g. star graph).

dfs.name: Depth-First Search (DFS)
dfs.purpose: Graph traversal exploring as deeply as possible along each branch before backtracking.
dfs.problem_statement: Traverse tree or graph along a path until dead end is reached, then backtrack.
dfs.intuition: Navigating a hedge maze with your hand on one wall: keep moving forward until you hit a dead end, then turn back.
dfs.worked_example: Start S -> go to neighbor A -> go to A's neighbor C -> dead end -> backtrack to A -> go to D.
advantages: Low memory when tree/graph has high branching factor but shallow goal.
Basis for topological sort and cycle detection.
limitations: Can wander down infinite or very long suboptimal paths.
Does not guarantee shortest route.
dfs.suitable_use_cases: Topological sorting, finding strongly connected components, maze generation, cycle detection.
common_mistakes: Claiming DFS finds shortest path (it does not).
Stack overflow in deep recursion without cycle protection.
dfs.exam_observations: Classifies graph edges into Tree, Back, Forward, and Cross edges.

dijkstra.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
dijkstra.purpose: Find the shortest paths from a single source to all vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights.
dijkstra.problem_statement: Given graph G with edge weights w(u,v) >= 0, find minimum cost path from source to target.
dijkstra.intuition: Greedy strategy: always finalize the unvisited vertex with the smallest known tentative distance from start.
dijkstra.worked_example: Dist[S]=0, others=inf. Pop S (d=0), relax neighbors A(d=4), B(d=2). Pop B (d=2), relax A via B: 2+1=3 < 4, update Dist[A]=3.
dijkstra.time_complexity: O((V + E) log V) with Min-Heap
dijkstra.space_complexity: O(V) for distance table and priority queue
dijkstra.stability: Guarantees optimal shortest path for non-negative weights.
advantages: Optimal lowest cost path.
Works with arbitrary positive edge weights.
limitations: Fails with negative edge weights (requires Bellman-Ford).
Explores in all directions without target guidance.
dijkstra.suitable_use_cases: GPS navigation, network packet routing protocols (OSPF).
common_mistakes: Using with negative edge weights, which breaks the greedy invariant.
Not updating visited set on pop.
dijkstra.exam_observations: Greedy choice property holds because edge weights are non-negative.

astar.name: A* Search
astar.purpose: Informed heuristic search finding the lowest-cost path from start to target.
astar.problem_statement: Evaluate nodes using f(n) = g(n) + h(n) where g is exact cost and h is admissible heuristic.
astar.intuition: Combines Dijkstra's cost-from-start with Greedy Best-First's goal-directed heuristic to search directly toward the target.
astar.worked_example: Node A has g=5, h=3 -> f=8. Node B has g=2, h=8 -> f=10. A* expands A first because f=8 < 10.
astar.time_complexity: O(E log V) average; worst case O(b^d)
astar.space_complexity: O(V) stores all generated nodes in open/closed lists
astar.stability: Guarantees optimal path if heuristic h(n) is admissible (never overestimates).
advantages: Significantly fewer node expansions than Dijkstra.
Guaranteed optimal with admissible heuristic.
limitations: Memory bound: stores all frontier and visited nodes.
Heuristic must be carefully designed.
astar.suitable_use_cases: Video game pathfinding, robotics motion planning, map navigation.
common_mistakes: Using an inadmissible heuristic (overestimating true distance), which sacrifices optimality.
astar.exam_observations: If h(n) = 0 everywhere, A* becomes identical to Dijkstra's algorithm.

nqueens.name: N-Queens Backtracking
nqueens.purpose: Place N chess queens on an N×N board such that no two queens attack each other.
nqueens.problem_statement: Find assignments (row, col) for N queens with no sharing of row, column, or diagonal.
nqueens.intuition: Construct candidate solutions row by row. Whenever a conflict is detected, prune the entire branch and backtrack.
nqueens.worked_example: For N=4: Queen 0 placed at (0, 1). Queen 1 placed at (1, 3). Queen 2 placed at (2, 0). Queen 3 placed at (3, 2). Solution found!
nqueens.space_complexity: O(N) for recursion stack and position arrays
advantages: Prunes dead-end subtrees early, drastically reducing search space compared to brute force O(N^N).
Finds all valid solutions.
limitations: Exponential worst-case runtime; intractable for large N (e.g. N > 25).
nqueens.suitable_use_cases: Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP), circuit routing, compiler register allocation.
common_mistakes: Re-checking rows when queens are already placed strictly one per row.
nqueens.exam_observations: For N=8, there are 92 total distinct solutions (12 fundamental symmetry solutions).
